title: Why does gRPC rely on HTTP/2 instead of HTTP/1.1, and what breaks with HTTP/1.1 (no multiplexing/streaming/binary)?
shortTitle: Why does gRPC rely on HTTP/2 instead of HTTP/1.1, and what breaks with HTTP/1.1 (no multiplexing/streaming/binary)?

s1_definition.profdef: gRPC depends on HTTP/2 because its core capabilities map directly onto HTTP/2 features that HTTP/1.1 lacks. HTTP/2 provides stream multiplexing (many concurrent, independent request/response streams over one TCP connection), full-duplex bidirectional streaming, a binary framing layer, and header compression. gRPC uses these for its four call types, long-lived streaming RPCs, trailers for status, and efficient concurrency. HTTP/1.1 is a text-based, request/response protocol with head-of-line blocking per connection, no true multiplexing, no server-initiated streaming within a single request, and no trailers, so gRPC's streaming and concurrency model cannot be expressed on it.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the line between the transfers desk and the accounts desk at National Bank of India. HTTP/1.1 is like a single phone line where you must finish one whole call before starting the next, and you cannot talk and listen continuously at the same time. HTTP/2 is like a modern switchboard on one wire that carries dozens of calls at once, each independent, and lets both sides talk simultaneously. gRPC was designed for busy, streaming, two-way conversations between desks, so it needs the switchboard. On the old single-call line, its streaming and many-calls-at-once features simply cannot happen.
s1_definition.oneliner: gRPC needs HTTP/2's multiplexing, bidirectional streaming, binary framing, and trailers; HTTP/1.1 lacks all of these, so gRPC's streaming and concurrency model cannot run on it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** gRPC depends on HTTP/2 because its core capabilities map directly onto HTTP/2 features that HTTP/1.1 lacks. HTTP/2 provides stream multiplexing (many concurrent, independent request/response streams over one TCP connection), full-duplex bidirectional streaming, a binary framing layer, and header compression. gRPC uses these for its four call types, long-lived streaming RPCs, trailers for status, and efficient concurrency. HTTP/1.1 is a text-based, request/response protocol with head-of-line blocking per connection, no true multiplexing, no server-initiated streaming within a single request, and no trailers, so gRPC's streaming and concurrency model cannot be expressed on it.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the line between the transfers desk and the accounts desk at National Bank of India. HTTP/1.1 is like a single phone line where you must finish one whole call before starting the next, and you cannot talk and listen continuously at the same time. HTTP/2 is like a modern switchboard on one wire that carries dozens of calls at once, each independent, and lets both sides talk simultaneously. gRPC was designed for busy, streaming, two-way conversations between desks, so it needs the switchboard. On the old single-call line, its streaming and many-calls-at-once features simply cannot happen.

**One line to remember:** gRPC needs HTTP/2's multiplexing, bidirectional streaming, binary framing, and trailers; HTTP/1.1 lacks all of these, so gRPC's streaming and concurrency model cannot run on it.

sections.s2_technical:
The first reason is multiplexing. HTTP/2 carries many logical streams over one TCP connection, each with its own stream id, interleaved as binary frames. This lets a single gRPC channel run many concurrent calls without opening many connections and without one slow call blocking others at the HTTP layer. HTTP/1.1 has no real multiplexing: a connection handles one request/response at a time, so clients resort to many parallel connections or pipelining, and pipelining suffers head-of-line blocking where a slow earlier response stalls later ones. gRPC's model of many concurrent RPCs on one channel relies on HTTP/2 multiplexing.

The second reason is streaming. gRPC's server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming need the ability to send a sequence of messages within a single logical call, in both directions, over time. HTTP/2 frames make this natural: DATA frames can flow in both directions on the same stream until it is closed. HTTP/1.1 fundamentally models one request then one response; you can approximate server push with chunked transfer encoding one way, but you cannot do true full-duplex bidirectional streaming within a single request, so gRPC's bidi and client-streaming calls cannot be represented.

The third reason is the binary framing layer. HTTP/2 is binary by design, which matches gRPC's binary Protocol Buffers payloads and its need to frame length-prefixed messages efficiently. HTTP/1.1 is text-oriented with textual headers, which is less efficient and not aligned with gRPC's framing. The fourth reason is trailers: gRPC communicates the final call status (the grpc-status code and message) in HTTP trailing headers sent after the response body, which is essential for streaming because the status is only known after all messages are sent. HTTP/1.1 does not support trailers reliably, so gRPC's status-after-stream mechanism breaks. HTTP/2 also brings HPACK header compression, reducing overhead for the many small metadata headers gRPC uses. Senior nuances: this HTTP/2 dependency is exactly why browsers cannot speak native gRPC (they do not expose raw HTTP/2 framing to JavaScript), which forces gRPC-Web plus a translating proxy like Envoy; it is also why some older load balancers and proxies that only understand HTTP/1.1, or that terminate HTTP/2 incorrectly, break gRPC, so you must ensure HTTP/2 end to end or use an L4 proxy. In practice I verify that every hop between gRPC peers preserves HTTP/2, otherwise multiplexing and streaming silently degrade or fail.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants a live statement feed where one request yields a continuous stream of transactions. On HTTP/1.1 this cannot be a true server stream within one call. This is exactly what HTTP/2 server streaming enables, and it is why gRPC requires HTTP/2.

Problem 2 — The transfer service fires many concurrent account calls and must not have them block each other at the HTTP layer. This is exactly what HTTP/2 multiplexing provides on a single channel, which HTTP/1.1 cannot.

The demo defines a server-streaming RPC that streams Rajesh's recent transactions over one call, demonstrating the HTTP/2 capability gRPC depends on. Classes and steps: `statement.proto` (server-streaming RPC), `StatementServiceImpl` (streams multiple responses on one call), and `StatementClient` (consumes the stream).

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a statement request for Rajesh's SAV2001.

Step 1 — The client opens one gRPC call over HTTP/2. HTTP/2 assigns this call a stream id, and because of multiplexing this stream coexists with any other concurrent calls on the same connection.

Step 2 — The server does not return one response; it emits three `TxnEntry` messages over time on the same open stream using DATA frames. This continuous one-to-many flow within a single call is possible only because HTTP/2 supports streaming; HTTP/1.1 could not model it as a true server stream.

Step 3 — After the last message, the server calls `onCompleted`, and gRPC sends the final grpc-status in HTTP/2 trailers, which arrive after the body. HTTP/1.1 lacks reliable trailers, so this status-after-stream pattern would break.

Step 4 — The client iterates the stream, logging each transaction and running balance as it arrives, never waiting for all data to be buffered as a single response.

```
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] Streaming statement for SAV2001
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] T1 Salary credit Rs.75000 bal=Rs.1075000
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] T2 Rent debit Rs.-25000 bal=Rs.1050000
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] T3 Transfer to CUR3001 Rs.-50000 bal=Rs.1000000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  HTTP/2 single connection
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ stream 1 ─── gRPC StreamStatement (server stream)
  │   client req "SAV2001"
  │   ◀ DATA frame TxnEntry T1
  │   ◀ DATA frame TxnEntry T2        (full-duplex, over time)
  │   ◀ DATA frame TxnEntry T3
  │   ◀ TRAILERS grpc-status=OK       (status AFTER body)
  │ stream 3 ─── another concurrent RPC (multiplexed, not blocked)
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  HTTP/1.1 (what breaks):
 no multiplexing   → one call blocks the connection
 no true streaming → cannot send T1,T2,T3 on one call
 no trailers       → cannot send grpc-status after body
 text framing      → mismatched with binary Protobuf
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — HTTP/2 Requirement Across Hops ═══

  ┌──────────┐ gRPC-Web ┌────────────────┐ gRPC/HTTP2 ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Browser  │─────────→│ Envoy proxy     │───────────→│ Statement Svc(×N) │
  │ (no raw  │  (HTTP/2  │ translates web  │  preserved  │ server streaming  │
  │  HTTP/2) │   bridge) │ → native gRPC   │  end-to-end │                   │
  └──────────┘          └────────────────┘             └──────────────────┘
  CRITICAL: every hop must preserve HTTP/2; an HTTP/1.1-only proxy breaks streaming.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — HTTP/2 Features gRPC Uses ═══

  ┌─ Why HTTP/2 (mapped to gRPC need) ────────────────────────────┐
  │ Multiplexing   → many concurrent RPCs on one channel          │
  │ Bidi streaming → client/server/bidi stream call types         │
  │ Binary framing → compact Protobuf, length-prefixed messages    │
  │ Trailers       → grpc-status after a streamed body            │
  │ HPACK          → compress many small metadata headers          │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: StatementServiceImpl only streams statements                │
  │ O: new streaming rpc = extend proto, no transport change       │
  │ D: client depends on generated streaming stub                  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. stub.streamStatement(req) → one HTTP/2 stream opened
  2.   → server obs.onNext(T1), onNext(T2), onNext(T3)
  3.   → obs.onCompleted() → HTTP/2 trailers grpc-status=OK
  4.   → client iterator consumes each entry as it arrives
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
gRPC relies on HTTP/2 because its core features map directly onto HTTP/2 capabilities that HTTP/1.1 simply does not have. HTTP/2 gives stream multiplexing, so many independent RPCs run concurrently over one connection without blocking each other at the HTTP layer. It gives full-duplex bidirectional streaming, so a single logical call can carry a sequence of messages in both directions over time. It is binary by design, which matches gRPC's binary Protocol Buffers and length-prefixed framing. And it supports trailers, which gRPC uses to send the final status code after a streamed body. It also brings HPACK header compression for the many small metadata headers gRPC uses.

On HTTP/1.1, several things break. There is no real multiplexing, so a connection handles one request and response at a time, and pipelining suffers head-of-line blocking where a slow response stalls later ones, which defeats gRPC's many-concurrent-calls model. There is no true full-duplex bidirectional streaming within one request, so gRPC's client-streaming and bidirectional calls cannot be represented, and even server streaming can only be faked with chunked encoding one direction. There are no reliable trailers, so gRPC's status-after-stream mechanism cannot work. And the text-oriented framing is mismatched with gRPC's binary payloads.

In my banking work at National Bank of India I used a server-streaming statement feed, where one request for Rajesh's account yields a continuous stream of transaction entries on a single call, with the final status delivered in trailers. That pattern only exists because of HTTP/2 streaming and trailers. At the same time the transfer service fires many concurrent account calls over one multiplexed channel without them blocking each other, which again is HTTP/2 multiplexing.

The senior point I always add is that this HTTP/2 dependency is exactly why browsers cannot speak native gRPC, since they do not expose raw HTTP/2 framing to JavaScript, so we use gRPC-Web with a translating proxy like Envoy, and it is why I verify HTTP/2 is preserved on every hop, because an older HTTP/1.1-only proxy or an incorrectly terminating load balancer will silently break multiplexing and streaming. So my summary answer is: gRPC needs HTTP/2's multiplexing, bidirectional streaming, binary framing, and trailers, and because HTTP/1.1 lacks every one of those, gRPC's streaming and concurrency model cannot run on it.
